The eleven ratings for Solid State

Investment memo · Solid State plc (SOLI-GB) · 24 October 2026

Solid State (SOLI-GB): a sound but under-earning defence integrator on a trough multiple, where one confirmed contract re-rates the shares and one deferral cuts them

Written on 24 October 2026 for Richard. The share price is 162.5p (22 October 2026), the market capitalisation about £98.5m and the enterprise value about £96m. Solid State's financial year ends on 31 March, so FY27 is the year now running. Returns are measured from 162.5p unless stated otherwise. Definitions of the profit basis, of consensus and of the base case are in the end-notes.

Three dated events fall within the next eight weeks: a trading update expected in early November, the first Capital Markets Day on 25 November, and the H1 FY27 results on 15 December. This memo is written to prepare Richard for those three events.

The case in one paragraph. Solid State is a £98m UK electronics integrator, accredited for defence, medical and industrial work, whose operating profit depends on one thing: how fully it uses a £42m overhead. Management built that overhead in FY26 for a £250m business, but revenue is £154m, and part of that revenue arrives in government-sized programme tranches whose timing the company does not control. The recurring revenue base (about £131m, growing 5% to 6% a year) and the two smaller divisions, Power and Components, are enough to support the level of the FY28 and FY29 forecasts; the programme revenue of the Systems division alone sets how wide the range of outcomes is around any single year. The shares have fallen 18% from 199p since the FY26 results in June while sell-side estimates have not changed, taking the two-year-forward P/E to 11.5x, the first percentile of the stock's own five-year range, at a time when every peer's rating has risen. The market has priced the fear of a repeat of November 2024, when a procurement review paused an order and the house broker cut EPS by 60% in one note. The market has not been shown the size of the prize if there is no repeat: each £10m of Systems revenue is worth about £3m of operating profit, or about 3.9p of EPS, a third of this year's earnings. Because the multiple is at a trough, the estimates have not been cut and the price moves only on the company's own news (the six-month R-squared to its peer basket is 1%), a single confirmed contract would produce an estimate upgrade and a re-rating at the same time, while a single deferral would cut estimates from an uncut level into a price that is already fearful. The expected 18-month return is favourable: about +35% probability-weighted, and +52% in the base case at the guideline multiple of 12.7x. The distribution of outcomes is bimodal, with roughly a one-in-five chance of a 40% fall. Richard should hold both facts at once.

The decision in three lines.

1. The expectation is favourable and dated: about +35% probability-weighted over 18 months, decided by three events in the next eight weeks.

2. The shape is bimodal: size the position for a one-in-five chance of a 40% fall, not for the average outcome.

3. The three-year return (+82% in the base case, mostly from earnings) survives a one-year deferral; the 18-month return (mostly from the multiple) does not.

The ten things that matter most.

1

Three engines drive growth, but one engine carries the risk. In the base case, operating profit rises from £9.6m in FY26 to £14.3m in FY29, and £4.0m of that £4.7m increase comes from Power (+£2.6m) and Components (+£1.4m). The drivers of those two divisions (United States autonomy orders, the industrial restock and contactors for AI data centres) do not depend on the Ministry of Defence. However, if no defence tranche ships in FY28 or FY29, Systems profit falls by about £5m, which equals the whole planned increase in group operating profit. The level of the forecast therefore rests on three divisions, while its predictability rests on one, Systems.

2

The base case is a staircase: FY27 is flat, FY28 steps up, and the H1 FY27 revenue decline is already known. The H1 FY27 results on 15 December will show revenue down about 12%, to about £75.5m, because H1 FY26 included a £23.3m NATO programme that does not repeat. Informed investors know this; stock screens may not. The real test in those results is the adjusted operating margin: the base case expects 5.6%, against a level of 5.5% below which the thesis is at risk. The base case puts FY27 EPS at 10.8p against consensus of 11.6p, because it weights the second-half tranche at 55% while the broker assumes the tranche in full. The base case puts FY28 EPS at 14.0p against consensus of 13.1p, because revenue that slips out of FY27 lands in FY28, on top of rising utilisation of the Ashchurch site. Consensus therefore has the right direction and the wrong shape.

3

The Defence Investment Plan has been published, and its publication did not lift the shares. Both earlier rounds of this analysis waited for the plan, which arrived on 30 June 2026: £298bn over four years, defence spending of 2.7% of GDP by 2029, and Projects CAIN and EVE named among the tactical radio programmes. The shares then fell 18%. The catalyst is now a contract, not a plan, and the risk has moved to the funding behind the plan: a £28bn gap between the Ministry of Defence's requirement and the Treasury's envelope, a spending review that may slip to autumn 2027, and a shelved target of 3% of GDP by 2030. The procurement machinery, by contrast, has improved. A £727m Tactical Communication Systems Framework (RM6393) was confirmed in August 2026; the Segmented Acquisition Model now offers a one-year route for upgrades to tactical communications; and the typical lag of three to six months from plan to supplier revenue points to contracts being signed in the current quarter.

4

Nobody has published the operating-leverage arithmetic. Break-even revenue is about £110m to £115m, given a 33.5% gross margin and £36m to £38m of fixed overhead. About £20m of recurring revenue, the size of one programme tranche, therefore separates the current revenue run-rate from zero operating profit. In the other direction, each £10m of Systems revenue adds about 190 basis points to group operating margin without new capital. The broker names utilisation as the profit lever but has published neither number, so the market knows the direction of the gearing but not its size in either direction.

5

The company, not the sector, drives the share's multiple. Over six months, the stock's beta to its fifteen dashboard peers is 0.21 and its R-squared is 1%; in the 2024 to 2025 deferral window the beta was negative. The de-rating, from 15x to 19x in the 2021 to 2024 delivery years to 11.5x now, reflects two things: fear about the timing of orders, and illiquidity on London's Alternative Investment Market (AIM), where about £0.3m of the shares trade a day. Company events can reverse both causes; a rise in sector ratings cannot. A sector re-rating therefore gives Solid State nothing, while a confirmed tranche gives it an upgrade and a re-rating at once.

6

The share price implies roughly double Viewforth's probability of a deferral. Taking the model's 18-month base-case value of 247p and a deferral-case value of about 95p, discounted back one year, the current price implies that the market attaches roughly a 40% to 45% probability to the deferral case, against Viewforth's 20%. The gap between those two probabilities is the mispricing in one number. The gap is also a warning, because the market has already watched this company suffer a deferral once.

7

Guidance is honest and conservative in level but silent on timing, and the Capital Markets Day will not end that silence. The company issues no numeric guidance; it adopts the average of its three brokers' forecasts and beats that average by 3% to 9% in normal years. Its 13 October announcement of the 25 November event says that no new financial information will be disclosed, so the event will cover strategy (including the company's "3Cs" framework) and introduce the new chair rather than update the numbers. Investors will probably ask for an Ashchurch utilisation figure, a margin bridge and a capital-allocation framework, and will probably not receive them. The first announcement that can move the numbers up is the April 2027 pre-close statement, the company's habitual point for upgrades.

8

The positives missing from the market's narrative outweigh the negatives missing from it.

Positives the market has not been told

  • The leverage arithmetic, in both directions
  • The FY28 catch-up of revenue that slips out of FY27
  • A through-life support revenue tail on over 2,000 Royal Marines radios and the 16 Air Assault Brigade deployment, inferred at 15% to 20% of hardware value over five years
  • Net cash by March 2028, with no stated plan for spending it
  • The long-term incentive plan (LTIP) band of 11.5p to 16.0p of FY28 EPS, which signals management's own range of expectations
  • A demonstrated record of passing component inflation through to customers

Negatives the market has not been told

  • 40% of purchases are in dollars with no forward cover: about ±£0.8m of pre-tax profit for each 10% move in sterling
  • The disclosures on working capital and on bill-and-hold revenue
  • The quiet removal of the 12% group margin target from the annual report
9

The company's foundations are narrower than its tailwinds. A genuine but narrow moat (accreditation, design-in, sovereign capacity in both the UK and the United States, and the exclusive Persistent Systems radio channel) protects price and market share on programmes already won, but does not control the timing of new ones. The foundations carry four specific weaknesses. One customer provided 17% of FY26 revenue. The radio moat is also a dependency on a sole supplier whose channel terms are undisclosed. 39% of revenue is franchised distribution at a 4% margin. And management is competent, low-paid and insider-heavy, seven months into a succession forced by the death of the chief executive, with a defence-industry chair (formerly chief executive of Thales UK) as the one external upgrade.

10

The stock is Bottoming, at the boundary with Turning up. By the dashboard's rule the stock is in the Bottoming phase, at the boundary with Turning up. The multiple has priced the fear, and the fundamentals have turned (the underlying order book is £18m higher, three divisions are growing and the destock is over), but the estimates have not been cut, which is the one feature of a textbook bottom that this one lacks. The closest of Richard's six setups is "CfC (cause for concern) in quality cyclical at trough-on-trough, leading to reversion to normal": a trough multiple on a trough margin (6.2% against a 9.2% FY21 to FY24 average), with a cause for concern (procurement timing) that is dated and resolvable. The fit is real but not crisp: the quality is medium, a ministry's calendar sets the cycle rather than the economy, and the estimates are not yet at a trough.

Implication for decision-making. This is a timing-led case with two likely outcomes, a favourable expectation and a dated calendar. The constructive way to own the shares is to size the position for the one-in-five chance of a 40% drawdown, and to use three dated events as the test (table below). If two of the three tests pass, the stock should move from Bottoming to Turning up on unchanged numbers; if the margin test fails, the stock follows the November 2024 template. Measured from 162.5p, the base-case three-year return (+82%, mostly from earnings) is far more robust to a deferral than the 18-month return (+52%, mostly from the multiple), because in this company's record a deferred order has so far been delayed, not lost.

The four judgements that move the value of the shares, with the arithmetic

Each judgement is measured against the base case. EPS effects use a 25% tax rate on 57.8m (FY27) or 58.1m (FY28) diluted shares.

Judgement 1: when the next Systems programme tranche ships (the dominant driver). The base case carries £13m of programme revenue in FY27 and £15m to £20m a year from FY28. The FY27 figure is Project CAIN's £8.0m initial order, shipped in the quarter to June 2026, plus a probability-weighted follow-on of about £5m in H2 (55% of about £9m). Systems revenue carries a 38.7% gross margin, and the standing costs of the Ashchurch site (about £3m a year, with £15m of unused revenue capacity) are already in the base case, so a tranche converts to operating profit at about 30% of its revenue.

  • If the weighted H2 FY27 tranche slips to April 2027: revenue falls £5m and operating profit £1.5m (from £9.2m to £7.7m, a 5.2% margin); net income falls £1.1m and EPS 1.9p, to about 8.9p. Consensus at 11.6p would then be 30% too high, and the sell side's habit (shown in November 2024) is to cut both years rather than move the revenue into the next year.
  • If FY27 repeats the full FY25 template (no tranche, wider slippage and under-absorbed overhead): revenue is about £142m, the margin 4.3% and EPS 7.0p; FY28 EPS then falls to 11.0p, which is the LTIP threshold.
  • If FY28 receives only £5m of the £15m to £20m programme block: revenue falls £10m, operating profit £3m and EPS 3.9p, to about 10.1p. If instead a brigade-scale tranche is £10m larger than planned, EPS rises 3.9p, to about 17.9p. This one revenue line therefore spans FY28 EPS of 10p to 18p around 14p, roughly ±28%; no other single line moves FY28 EPS by nearly as much (the next largest, overhead growth, moves it by about ±1.4p).

Judgement 2: how fast overhead grows once the tranches arrive (the net operating leverage). The base case has adjusted overhead rising from £42.0m in FY26 to £42.2m in FY27, £44.4m in FY28 (+5.2%) and £46.4m in FY29, which leaves 21% to 25% of incremental revenue reaching operating profit after reinvestment. In FY26 management reinvested about 70% of a £12.2m gain in gross profit (overhead rose £8.7m), and nothing yet shows that the new chief executive will reinvest at a slower pace.

  • FY28 overhead grows 7.5% (half an FY26-sized step) to £45.4m: operating profit falls £1.0m and EPS 1.3p, to 12.7p, which is the bottom of the brokers' range.
  • FY28 overhead is held to inflation (+2.5%) at £43.3m: operating profit rises £1.1m and EPS 1.4p, to 15.4p.
  • Overhead growth two points a year faster or slower compounds to about ±£2.3m of operating profit by FY29, about ±3p on FY29 EPS of 17.7p.

Judgement 3: whether memory and semiconductor cost inflation is recovered in full, and how quickly (gross margin). The base case has gross margin at 33.6% in FY27 (+40 basis points from mix, −30 basis points from the lag in passing costs through) and 33.8% in FY28. DRAM contract prices rose about 60% in the second quarter of 2026 and a further 13% to 18% in the third, and the company has said that some programmes could become "temporarily unviable" at the new prices. Each 50 basis points of gross margin on £153m of revenue is £0.77m of operating profit, about 1.0p of EPS.

  • FY27 gross margin of 32.6% (the lag not recovered within the year, and price-sensitive Components customers refusing increases): EPS falls 2.0p, to about 8.8p.
  • FY27 gross margin of 34.0% (allocation pricing kept, as specialist distributors managed in 2021 to 2023): EPS rises 0.8p, to 11.6p, the consensus figure.
  • The cash cost is separate: each £5m of extra strategic stock adds £5m of net debt (the model's lease-inclusive net debt at March 2027 rises from £8.5m to £13.5m) and about £0.3m of interest, or 0.4p of EPS.

The 2021 to 2023 record sets the weight of Judgement 3. Through a shortage with 50-week lead times, the company reported "practically zero impact" on gross margin. That record says the gross-margin outcome is well protected and the timing outcome is exposed, which is why the gross-margin risk sits largely inside Judgement 1's range rather than adding to it.

Judgement 4: the multiple the market will pay once the first tranche is confirmed, or if it is not (the lifecycle phase). The guideline fair multiple is 12.7x two-year-forward EPS, the 30th percentile of the stock's own ten-year range, applied at the model's 18-month column; the model's 18-month value of 247p rests on it. Each turn of multiple on the forward earnings the model uses at September 2027 (about 19p to 20p) is worth about 19p a share, 12% of today's price.

  • 10.9x (the ten-year tenth percentile, the "crash" band): about 212p, still +30%, because earnings growth does the rest.
  • 12.7x (the guideline): 247p, +52%.
  • 14.1x (the ten-year median, the level the stock held through 2022 to 2024): about 275p, +69%.
  • Deferral: forward EPS falls to about 11p (FY28), and the market has twice capitalised the depressed current-year earnings rather than the recovery year (in December 2024 the price reached 123p, 17x a cut FY26 figure). 12x to 14x on 7p of FY27 EPS gives 85p to 100p; a calmer market paying 11x FY28 EPS gives about 120p. The deferral range is therefore 85p to 120p, a fall of 26% to 48%.

A fifth judgement, the Power division's margin path from 5.3% to 10% by FY30, is real but second-order: a stall at 6% in FY28 would cost about £0.8m of operating profit, or 1.0p of EPS.
