1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds and risks

Key messageDemand for Solid State's products is structural and larger over three years; the headwinds (input costs, Treasury funding, the dollar) are more certain over the next six months.

Evidence: the tailwinds. Defence and security provided 47% of FY26 revenue (£72.5m, up 25%), against about 30% in FY25, so the defence budget cycle now drives nearly half of the group. Five demand forces support the business (figure below): rising defence budgets, a doctrine that points procurement at Solid State's products, a filling order book in the tier of suppliers below the prime contractors, the end of the industrial destock, and a small new leg in AI data centres and autonomy.

Evidence: the headwinds. The headwinds are certain where the tailwinds are dated. The most important is input cost: cost of sales is two-thirds of revenue, so a 5% unrecovered rise in bought-in costs would remove more than half of operating profit. Treasury funding, procurement screening, the United States budget process and the unhedged dollar complete the list.

Inference. The demand forces are structural at the budget level and aimed precisely at Solid State's products, which is rare for a £98m company. The conversion of budgets into tranches, however, runs on a calendar that has slipped once and is contested at the Treasury. That conversion now has a measurable lag: three to six months from plan to supplier revenue, which points to contracts in October to December 2026 and shipments in the fourth quarter of FY27, exactly where the base case places its weighted £5m. The supply headwind is the more certain force over six months; the demand tailwind is the larger force over three years.

So what. Model demand as a rising trend with a wide timing band, not as a smooth line. Carry a gross-margin band of 32% to 34%, and the working-capital build that protects it. Treat the industrial restock as a pulse of six to eighteen months, worth mid-single-digit growth in Components and plateauing by the end of calendar 2026, not as a compounding driver.

Strongest counter-case. The bear reading of the same evidence (one AlphaSense inference, rated low confidence) is that the next phase of CAIN slips to late 2027. In that reading, the Treasury prioritises the nuclear deterrent and long-cycle platforms over tactical radios, the CMA screening adds months to every award, and the restock peaks in the December quarter just as Solid State's weak year-on-year comparison is most visible. The three tailwinds would then arrive in FY29, and the company would spend FY27 and FY28 carrying £3m a year of idle Ashchurch overhead and a rising stock of memory parts.

What would change my view. Up: a contract notice under RM6393, or under the Land Environment Tactical Communication and Information Systems line, naming Wave Relay or Steatite; a first follow-on order from the NATO Support and Procurement Agency outside the UK; an Autumn Budget that funds the plan's conventional lines. Down: a formal delay to the spending review with defence lines deferred; a company statement that a programme has been deferred because of component cost; a weak restock read-across from discoverIE's results on 2 December.

Against the market. The consensus narrative (Zeus) headlines the defence tailwind and the restock but models neither as a number. It has not registered that the plan it was waiting for has been published, that the £727m framework vehicle now exists, or that the Treasury funding gap is the new risk. I agree with the market that the tailwinds exceed the headwinds over three years. I disagree that the clearing event is still ahead: the plan has been published, it cleared nothing, and the next clearing event is a contract.

Score: 58. Structural, well-aimed demand tailwinds in defence and a cyclical turn in industrial, offset by a certain input-cost headwind and a conversion calendar the company does not control.

2Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems and risks

Key messageThe organisation has changed a great deal and the financial levers not at all: the changes raise the payoff once tranches arrive, and the cost of waiting until they do.

Evidence: leadership. Within seven months the company lost its chief executive of twenty years (Gary Marsh died in November 2025), promoted John Macmichael, head of Components for twenty years, to permanent chief executive from 26 March 2026 (base salary £261,000, bottom-decile for the sector), and recruited Victor Chavez CBE, former chief executive of Thales UK, as chair from 27 June 2026. Chavez bought 12,500 shares at 159p on joining.

Evidence: structure, commercial model and capacity. The group was simplified into three accountable divisions with medium-term margin targets (Systems 12.5% to 15.0%, Power 10.0% to 14.0%, Components 7.0% to 9.0%). Separating Power made visible a business whose margin rose from 1.0% to 5.3% in a year by exiting commodity assembly. The commercial model was redirected toward programmes and own-brand products, supported by a Commercial Project Office, a group Chief Technology Officer, a Chief Relationship Officer and a United States Chief Sales Officer. Capacity was built ahead of revenue: the Ashchurch site, a near-field radio-frequency test chamber, United States antenna production and Power test rooms, with capital expenditure above £7.5m across FY27 and FY28, about double the consensus line. The broker base widened (Berenberg initiated coverage in December 2025; Zeus became joint broker from 1 October 2026), and the first Capital Markets Day is dated.

Evidence: insider behaviour. Insiders have bought and not sold: Chavez in December 2025, and Jon Baxter (head of Solsta) 9,500 shares at 178.45p in September 2026. The October 2026 dealings were Bed-and-ISA transfers and option exercises, neutral for net ownership. 600,375 options lapsed in May 2026 when targets were missed, rather than being reset, and the AGM re-elected the chief executive with 99.85% of votes cast.

Evidence: what did not change. The financial machinery is untouched: no numeric guidance, no capital return, no acquisition step-up, and a cost base growing ahead of revenue (detail in the right-hand column below).

Inference. The internal changes are coherent and already paid for, but on their own they cannot move the numbers. What they do is raise the payoff from external forces once the tranches arrive, because the new capacity lets each £10m of Systems revenue drop through to operating profit at about 30%, and raise the cost of waiting, at £2m to £3m a year of unabsorbed overhead.

The succession produced an operator to keep the business running and a chair chosen to open Ministry of Defence doors. That is the right pairing for a case whose binding constraint is access to procurement rather than engineering.

Two signals deserve weight because they are the only numbers management issues: the quiet withdrawal of the 12% margin target and the low LTIP threshold. Together they say that management regards near-flat earnings over the next two years as possible, and the direction to 2030 as settled.

So what. Treat the FY27 cost base as largely in place. Treat the Capital Markets Day as the one internal event that can change the case within six months, and rank its possible content by value: an Ashchurch utilisation figure first, then the fate of the 12% target, then the programme and support share of Systems revenue, then a capital-allocation framework. The company has said in advance that it will give no new financial information, so the base expectation should be frameworks, and any number would be upside to the narrative.

Strongest counter-case. Four facts argue that the change is weaker than it looks. A long-serving insider on bottom-decile pay, with a UK-centred career, is running a United States expansion from Worcestershire, while a 71% rise in administrative headcount sits oddly with an engineering culture. The one large acquisition of the last five years (Custom Power, for up to $45m) took three years and a £2.7m impairment to fix. The finance director, in post since 2017, is rated a high key-person risk. And management's demonstrated response to a downturn (£1m of savings within months in late 2024, against a £12m fall in gross profit) shows the cost base is built to grow into, not to flex.

What would change my view. Up: a numeric profit bridge or a utilisation figure at the Capital Markets Day, despite the "no new financial information" caveat; a stated leverage range or buyback authority; an external senior hire in the United States. Down: a reframing of the 2030 ambition around revenue without a margin path; FY27 overhead above £42.2m at the June 2027 results; the finance director's departure.

Against the market. The market reads the chair's appointment as a credential and the Capital Markets Day as a margin story (Zeus, after its October site visit, calls the margin opportunity "material"). I agree on the direction. I think the market over-expects numbers in November and under-weights two signals management has already sent: the wide FY28 range in its incentive plan and the withdrawn group margin target in its annual report.

Score: 52. Real, coherent, pre-funded organisational change with a defence-access chair, offset by the absence of any financial change force (no guidance, no capital return, no acquisition step-up) and a cost base growing ahead of revenue.

3Value chain and industry structure; business model, competitive advantage and barriers; financial profile; management

Key messageThe moat is genuine but narrow: about 61% of revenue sits in accredited niches, part of that moat belongs to a sole-source supplier, and the other 39% of revenue has no moat.

Evidence on structure: the accredited niches. About 61% of revenue (Systems and Power) sits in qualified niches where accreditation, not price, decides competition. The barriers are AS9100 and ISO 13485 certification, Official Secrets Act clearances, Secure by Design, systems compliant with the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), and design-in lives of seven to thirty years. Each niche is a local oligopoly, and margins there move with utilisation, not with pricing: that is why FY25's 23% revenue fall left gross margin at 31.5% while operating margin halved.

Evidence on structure: the distribution leg. The other 39% of revenue (Solsta distribution) sits in a fragmented stage of the value chain that is being disintermediated: semiconductor makers sell direct, Asian optoelectronics makers price into medical lasers, and AI design tools erode the value of application engineering. Solsta's 4.0% operating margin is the result of that structure.

Evidence on structure: the dependencies above the company. The main fragility sits above Solid State in the supply chain, not beside it. Persistent Systems is the exclusive and sole source of the MPU5 radios and Wave Relay networks behind CAIN and the NATO deliveries, on undisclosed channel terms. Expert benchmarks put programme-level channel margins near 10% and value-added integration at 20% to 25%; Systems' 38.7% gross margin says that Steatite earns an integrator's margin, not the radio maker's. The radio makers' own economics are far richer: Silvus, another tactical-radio maker, earned a 45% EBITDA margin and was bought by Motorola for $4.4bn. Memory makers are rationing supply, and exposure to Taiwan is critical.

Evidence on structure: customer concentration. One customer provided 17% of FY26 revenue (£26.7m), and one provided 20% in FY24. Concentration above 15% is therefore the signature of every year in which the thesis works.

Evidence on structure: category deal prices. Scaled acquirers are buying into these exact niches at 9x to 12x EBITA: discoverIE's purchases of Trival (antennas) and 3Gmetalworx (shielding), Diploma's purchase of CDM, the Cicor bid for TT Electronics, and a recommended cash offer for Gooch & Housego at 25.9x operating profit and a 41% premium. These deals put more resources behind competitors and set a price for the category. At about 7x FY27 EBITDA, Solid State is valued well below that price.

Evidence on the business model and advantage. The moat has five parts: accreditation; design-in irreversibility (a Steatite computer or Custom Power battery pack specified into a platform cannot be swapped without recertification); a sovereign UK and United States footprint that is new and under-used (Ashchurch with £15m of revenue headroom, Fountain Valley, and Q-Par USA's approved-supplier status); relationships with BAE Systems, Lockheed Martin, Saab, Siemens Healthcare and Philips; and the leading European training position for Wave Relay.

The moat protects price and share on programmes already won. It does not time new programmes, and it does not compound mechanically: the company discloses no design-win bank, churn, retention or utilisation metric, whereas discoverIE discloses a £385m design-win bank. Pricing power is cost recovery, not price leadership: the company passed 2021 to 2023 inflation through in full and passed tariffs through at a cost of 10 basis points. The gross-margin gap to discoverIE, about seven points, is structural.

Evidence on the financial profile. The profile is reliable at the gross line, depressed at the operating line and clean on the balance sheet; the earnings-quality flags sit in working capital (table below).

Evidence on management. Management is competent, honest, low-paid and insider-heavy. It sets a low bar and beats it. It explains the mechanism clearly (programmes fill Ashchurch, utilisation lifts the Systems margin, own-brand products lift gross margin) but discloses the numbers thinly. It cut the dividend in FY25 rather than pay it out of a weak year, then restored it covered four times by earnings, and no director has sold a share on the open market.

Governance is adequate rather than strong: there is no internal audit function during a United States expansion, independent directors are 43% of the board excluding the chair, the auditor has served for more than ten years, and the results platform allows live questions to be filtered. Ambition is large relative to the base (20p of EPS and £250m of revenue by 2030, and a 20% compound total shareholder return) but ordinary next to the step-changes Volex and discoverIE have delivered. Capital allocation is passive: management operates the business and generates cash, but does not allocate capital actively.

Inference. Solid State is a sub-tier supplier in a sovereign supply chain whose profit pool favours the designer and integrator, which Solid State partly is, and penalises the small distributor, which it also is. The industry structure gives it protected pricing and a benign set of competitors where it earns its margin, and leaves timing and input costs outside its control.

The financial profile is that of an asset-light accredited integrator carrying a fixed overhead sized for a larger business: a reliable gross margin, an operating margin that is cyclically depressed but mechanically recoverable through utilisation, middling returns on capital that double on tangible capital, and a balance sheet that acts as a buffer. Management is a reason to trust the gross margin, the cash and the expectation-setting; it is not a reason to expect any influence over the Ministry's calendar.

So what. Build the model from programme timing and utilisation, as the base case does. Model Components at low single-digit margins that rise only with own-brand mix. Treat the balance sheet as an unexercised option worth 8% to 12% of EPS (a £10m buyback at 165p would retire 10.5% of the shares). Treat work in progress and inventory, not the profit adjustments, as the earnings-quality signal to watch at each interim.

Strongest counter-case. The moat is narrower than it looks, for five reasons. Persistent Systems could sell direct or change channel terms on renewal, and the annual report itself lists loss of a distribution franchise as a principal risk. The Royal Marines programme that sources call "Project EVE" may be a conflation, which shows how thin the public record on the channel is. Thirteen sites on £154m of revenue is bottom-decile revenue per site, and management is not addressing it. The "false friend" profile (headline growth masking deterioration in working capital and capitalised costs) wins the competing-hypotheses analysis in the Risks report, and XP Power's collapse followed that pattern. And management has never shown an outlier standard on any disclosed operating metric.

What would change my view. Up: a disclosed programme or support share of Systems revenue, a utilisation figure, or any churn or retention metric; a renewal of the Persistent Systems agreement on stated multi-year terms; a Components margin above 5% on own-brand mix. Down: a direct UK entity or ministry relationship for Persistent Systems; a write-down of inventory or work in progress; a second United States impairment.

Against the market. The market credits the accreditation moat and the defence exposure. It does not price the two dependencies above the company (the channel partner and the memory makers) or the structural weakness of the distribution leg; nor does it price the takeover floor that recent category deal prices imply. I agree that the qualified niches are good businesses. I rate the group's foundations a notch below the market narrative, because 39% of revenue has no moat and part of the moat on the other 61% belongs to a supplier.

Score: 44. A genuine but narrow accreditation and design-in moat in sovereign niches, a bottom-of-cohort margin and return profile that is mechanically recoverable, a clean balance sheet, and competent rather than outlier management, in an industry structure that is supportive on price and unsupportive on timing and inputs.

4Conservatism of guidance; proactivity with the sell side; track record of delivery and upgrades

Key messageGuidance is honest and modestly sandbagged in level but silent on timing, the one factor that decides a year; the next upgrade point is the April 2027 pre-close, not the Capital Markets Day.

Evidence: how guidance works. The company issues no numeric guidance. It names its three covering brokers, adopts their average as "market expectations" and speaks to that average, so guidance and consensus are one number by construction. Its qualitative steer for FY27 is "margins broadly stable as investment continues ahead of revenue", with caveats that delays to the plan may affect order-book growth and that component shortages may affect project timing and viability. Against that steer, the chief executive spoke of "high confidence to exceed next-year market expectations" at the June results, and Zeus describes its own FY28 growth forecast of 2.6% as "prudently modelled with scope for upgrade".

Evidence: the delivery record. FY26 beat the original consensus by 6% on revenue and 19% on adjusted pre-tax profit, and beat the bar raised in April by 1% and 9%. FY24 met expectations, and FY22 and FY23 brought upgrades of more than 20% in several periods. FY25 missed the original expectation by 67% at the pre-tax line for an external reason (a customer's procurement review), then beat the rebased figure by 19%.

Evidence: when upgrades come. Upgrades come at two fixed points, the April pre-close and the June results, and on signed orders: in March 2025 the reinstated $25m order added 20% to FY26 EPS. The broker left its forecasts unchanged on the CAIN award and on $20m of Power orders, "on a prudent basis". The medium-term markers (20p of EPS, £250m of revenue and the divisional margins) are explicit, but the 12% group margin figure has gone. The LTIP band for FY28 is 11.5p to 16.0p, with a midpoint of 13.75p against consensus of 12.7p to 13.1p.

Inference. The guidance process is good in quality and small in quantity. It is honest and conservative in level; it is modestly sandbagged (a low bar beaten by 3% to 9%); it was rebased without a kitchen-sink write-down when the calendar moved; and it is silent on timing, the only factor that decides a year. The company's qualitative commentary runs ahead of the numbers on demand and behind them on timing, and the broker has written down the cautious side. Management's own central expectation for FY28, read from the LTIP midpoint and the June commentary, is modestly above consensus.

So what. Read FY27 consensus as management's cautious case for the level of demand, but not for its timing, which is why the base case sits below it. Read FY28 and FY29 consensus as a slope the company itself expects to beat. If the second half delivers, expect the next upgrade at the April 2027 pre-close and not before, because this management waits for the signed order.

Strongest counter-case. Conservative guidance is worth little when the miss, when it comes, is 60% in a month. The beats are small because the bar is set after the order book is known, and the one time the order book moved, the record offered no protection. A company that defines expectations as its brokers' average has, in effect, outsourced its guidance to a broker whose November 2024 note cut two years at once.

What would change my view. Up: a November trading update that says "in line", with an order book above £100m and a reference to second-half programme deliveries; an April 2027 pre-close that raises FY27, as the company did in March 2024 and April 2026. Down: a warning at the interim that FY27 is weighted to the second half; a Capital Markets Day that re-dates the divisional targets beyond 2030.

Against the market. Consensus has FY27 loaded into the second half without saying so, and has not modelled the deferral case at all. Over the events of the next 18 months, the FY27 expectation is more likely to be reduced (about 40%) than raised (20%), most likely by a modest phasing cut at the interim or the April pre-close; for FY28 the probabilities invert (raised: about 50%). I agree with the market that the company is an honest tracker that sandbags. I disagree that the current FY27 number is safe through the next two events.

Score: 52. An honest, conservative, modestly sandbagged guidance habit with a good record in normal years, undermined by one large miss when the customer's calendar moved and by the absence of any timing guidance now.

5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops: does revenue growth lead to outsized profit growth?

Key messageRevenue growth produces outsized profit growth through one mechanism only, fixed-cost absorption: a 10% revenue surprise in either direction moves EPS by roughly a third.

Evidence: fixed-cost operating leverage. Operating leverage is the largest in the cohort, and it has grown. In FY25 revenue fell 23% and adjusted operating profit fell 65%, so 29% of the lost revenue was lost as profit. In FY26 revenue rose 23% and gross profit captured 42% of the increase, but operating profit kept only 12% of it, because £8.7m of overhead was added. Fixed overhead is now about £4m higher than at the FY24 peak, so the revenue needed for a 10% operating margin has risen from about £163m to about £200m.

Gross leverage is about 40% of incremental revenue, and net leverage after reinvestment about 22% to 25%. When revenue slips, the decremental rate is close to the full gross rate, because there is no reinvestment that management can withdraw quickly.

Evidence: pricing power. Pricing power is cost recovery only. No company disclosure in five years attributes a gross-margin movement to price. The 2021 to 2023 shortage was passed through in full, with gross margin held in a band of 29% to 31.7%. Mix is what lifts the margin, by about 20 basis points a year: the Gateway product at 40% to 43% gross margin, antennas at 60% to 70% product margins, and the exit from low-value Power and Components work.

Evidence: financial leverage and cost-out. Financial leverage is immaterial and falling: net interest falls from about £0.9m in FY27 to £0.2m by FY31 as net debt turns to net cash by March 2028, and a 100 basis point move in interest rates is worth 0.1p of EPS. Cost-out is small: £0.5m to £1.0m a year of identifiable efficiencies is absorbed by the £0.5m cost of the Autumn Budget and by wage inflation, and the savings reach the gross-margin line rather than overhead. In a downturn, £2m to £3m of savings is reachable within six months and £4m to £6m within twelve.

Evidence: feedback loops. Four loops reinforce growth and four work against it; all of them act slowly (table below).

Inference. Fixed-cost absorption is both the attraction and the exposure. The other levers are either absent (price, financial gearing, cost-out) or slow (the feedback loops), so EPS growth should not be expected to decouple from Systems volume for at least two years. By FY29 the recurring share of Systems revenue may reach 10% to 15%, which is enough to narrow the range of outcomes but not to remove it.

So what. The base case's EPS growth of about 15% a year from FY26, on revenue growth of 5% to 6% and overhead growth of 4% to 5%, is the leverage working at a measured pace; it is not an aggressive margin assumption. If Richard believes the tranches will arrive, the base-case EPS is conservative (Judgement 2 shows about ±1.4p of FY28 EPS for two points of overhead growth). If he does not, no other lever rescues the year.

Strongest counter-case. Solid State has a manufacturer's operating leverage without a manufacturer's self-help. discoverIE's asset-light model held margins up through a 7% organic decline, and Volex and TT Electronics had structural inefficiencies to remove and removed them. Solid State has no inefficiency on that scale, and therefore no margin story independent of volume. The memory squeeze is also the one condition that tests a fixed-cost integrator's pass-through discipline harder than 2021 to 2023 did.

What would change my view. Up: H1 FY27 gross margin above 34% (evidence that higher prices are being kept); a disclosed support-revenue figure; overhead at the interim running at an annual rate below £42.2m. Down: gross margin below 33% at the interim; a statement that a programme was deferred because of component cost; a further step up in administrative headcount in the FY27 annual report.

Against the market. The market knows utilisation is the lever, but nobody has published the drop-through, the £110m to £115m break-even or the symmetry between upside and downside. The market over-fears the gross margin (nobody cites the 2021 to 2023 pass-through record) and under-fears the timing. I agree the leverage is material. My addition is that the leverage works as a staircase, in steps as tranches land, not as a slope, and that its downside is as steep as its upside.

Score: 58. Very high and mechanical fixed-cost operating leverage that converts each £10m of Systems revenue into about 190 basis points of group margin, with no pricing power, no financial gearing, little cost-out and slow loops, so the outsized profit growth depends on volume alone and runs in both directions.

6Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth, and for higher growth and margins than the past

Key messageDouble-digit EPS growth is available for four years from a trough, and it is organic and led by utilisation; the operating margin, however, only approaches its historic average in FY31.

Evidence: the record. From FY22 to FY26 revenue grew 16% a year compound (£85.0m to £154.1m, about half of it acquired), while adjusted EPS fell 6% a year (14.1p to 11.0p). Operating margin peaked at 10.4% in FY24 and troughed at 4.8% in FY25.

Evidence: the base case. The base case grows EPS about 15% a year compound from 11.0p, after a 2% dip in FY27, on revenue growth of 6% to 8% from FY28 (table below).

Evidence: the divisions, management's ambition and the cohort. Systems reaches the top of its margin target by FY29 and Power the bottom of its target by FY30, while Components never reaches its target (left-hand table below). Against management's 2030 ambition, the base case reaches 20p of EPS a year late and does not reach £250m of revenue (it reaches £190m to £200m). On consensus, Solid State's EPS growth is the lowest in its cohort in the first year and the most back-end loaded (right-hand table).

Inference. Double-digit EPS growth is available for four years from a trough, and it is a different kind of growth from that of the last six years: organic rather than acquired, led by utilisation rather than by programme spikes, and helped rather than hurt below the operating line by falling interest and a flat share count.

The operating margin does not regain the FY21 to FY24 average within the forecast, because the fixed cost base is £4m larger than at the last peak; EPS exceeds the FY24 peak of 20.0p only in FY30. "Higher growth and margins than the past" is therefore true of EPS growth and of gross margin, but not of operating margin, which recovers toward a normal level that is lower than history, on a larger capacity base.

The quality of the growth is better than its quantity suggests: free cash flow roughly doubles, net cash builds to about £16m by FY31 with nothing assumed for buybacks or acquisitions, and the recurring share of revenue rises.

So what. The base case is a central, probability-weighted path with explicit ranges (FY27 EPS 7p to 12p; FY28 EPS 11p to 17.5p). The award-led path (25% probability) runs a year ahead of it (FY28 17.5p, FY29 22.5p, meeting the 2030 ambition on time), and the deferral path (20%) runs a year behind (FY27 7.0p, FY28 11.0p, FY29 15p). The probability-weighted EPS sits below the base case in FY27 and above it from FY28, because the deferral risk is front-loaded and the award upside back-loaded.

Strongest counter-case. Half of the four-year path rests on capabilities not yet demonstrated: delivery of Tier 2 sub-systems at scale from a facility with one named award; pricing of a support tail whose channel terms are undisclosed; United States antenna manufacturing at a site that produced an impairment three years ago; and an engineering bench that has not grown. The precedents (Astra Microwave, XP Power's Vietnam site, TT Electronics' Cleveland site) show that loading new capacity with government serial volume does reach the target margin, but takes longer than planned and slips at least once. The base case assumes one slip is already inside its 55% weighting; a second slip would push 20p of EPS out to FY32.

What would change my view. Up: FY27 overhead at or below £42.2m with H2 revenue at or above £77.5m (the staircase confirmed); a disclosed support-revenue line. Down: FY27 gross margin below 33%; Systems revenue below £24m in H1 FY27; Power margin below 6% at the interim.

Against the market. The sell side models a smooth slope of margin (6.3%, 6.6%, 7.5%) on flat revenue, and its FY29 figure rests on one broker's estimate. I model a staircase in which FY27 is flat, below consensus this year and above it for the next two, and I treat FY29 consensus as a scenario rather than a forecast. We share the direction; we differ on the shape and on the FY28 level.

Score: 55. Fifteen per cent compound EPS growth from a trough on organic mid-single-digit revenue growth, with doubling free cash flow and a move to net cash, qualified by a flat first year, a margin that only regains its historic average in the final year, and a path half-dependent on capabilities not yet demonstrated.

7Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over the next 6 to 12 months

Key messageThe upgrade scope is about 10% on FY28 and FY29 EPS, dated to April and June 2027 and conditional on one contract; the near-term risk is a modest FY27 cut.

Evidence: where the gap lies. The base case is 6% below consensus EPS for FY27 and 9% and 14% above it for FY28 and FY29 (table below), so the arithmetic scope for upgrades lies in the later years and the arithmetic risk in the current one.

Evidence: how the sell side revises. The sell side revises at four points a year: the November update, the December interim, the April pre-close and the June results. It leaves forecasts unchanged on contract wins and strong interims, cuts across two years on a deferral, and rebuilds in one step on signature.

Evidence: the narrative is thin. One broker owns the narrative, and it is thin exactly where this memo's case is thick: nobody has articulated the leverage arithmetic, the tranche probability, the support tail, the pass-through record, the move to net cash or the capital-allocation option. The research pool contains no expert-call coverage of the company and no visible investor commentary. No regulatory notification of a holding has been made since the June results; with a free float of about 70%, the fall from 199p to 162p happened below the 3% disclosure threshold.

Evidence: Capital Markets Day precedents. The company has pre-announced that its Capital Markets Day will carry no new financial information. Peer events show the range of outcomes: Volex's April 2026 event gave numbers ($2bn and 12%) and brokers raised forecasts within days; discoverIE's September 2024 event gave a target, and its shares still de-rated with the cycle; TT Electronics' April 2024 event gave a target that execution problems then overwhelmed.

Inference: within six months. The scope for upgrades within six months is modest and lies in the narrative rather than the numbers. The Capital Markets Day can turn a story that is "specific in structure, vague in arithmetic" into something investors can monitor, but only if the question session yields a utilisation figure or a programme share, and management has signalled that it will not volunteer either.

Inference: within twelve months. The scope within twelve months is larger and dated. At the April 2027 pre-close, after the second-half tranche has or has not shipped, FY27 becomes known and FY28 forecasts move; the June 2027 results are the brokers' habitual point for raising the following year (June 2026 raised FY27 by 12.5%). If FY27 closes near 10.8p, the April statement will say "in line" or "slightly below", with FY28 held. If the tranche is larger than the weighted £5m, the statement will say "ahead", with FY28 raised toward 14p. In either base path, FY28 consensus moves toward the base case by June 2027 (probability about 55%).

Coverage will widen regardless: Zeus and Berenberg will publish FY29 and FY30 forecasts at or after the Capital Markets Day, probably below the base case in the brokers' habit, so the revision series will carry information for the first time.

So what. Expect the first FY27 revision after the interim to be down (probability about 35%) or nil (50%) rather than up (15%), and expect the dashboard's sell-side momentum grade to stay at D until April. Expect the narrative to change quickly once a number exists, because there is no entrenched wrong narrative to displace, only an absent one.

Strongest counter-case. A company that will not give numbers at its own first Capital Markets Day, with a broker that will not pre-empt an order, in a market that refuses re-ratings, may simply stay at 11x until a tranche is announced. The tranche's timing (three to six months after a plan whose funding is contested) can slip past April 2027, in which case the upgrade cycle starts a year later than this memo expects.

What would change my view. Up: a regulatory announcement of a CAIN follow-on or a NATO framework order before the interim (the company announces orders of this size); Zeus or Berenberg publishing FY29 EPS above 16p. Down: a Capital Markets Day that reframes the 2030 ambition around revenue without a margin path, which would take the one FY29 forecast down.

Against the market. The market expects the Capital Markets Day to be the catalyst. I expect the Capital Markets Day to be the stage and the April pre-close to be the catalyst, with the November order book and the December margin as the gates between them. I agree with the market that FY28 is where the upgrades lie. I would add that, with estimates uncut and the multiple at a trough, the upgrade will coincide with the re-rating rather than precede it.

Score: 50. Clear arithmetic scope for FY28 and FY29 upgrades of around 10%, dated to April and June 2027 and conditional on one contract, offset by a near-term skew toward a modest FY27 cut and a Capital Markets Day that has pre-announced it will not supply numbers.

8Current momentum in guidance, sell-side estimates, narrative and share-price technicals, and the same for key peers

Key messageEvery momentum reading is weak while the valuation is the cheapest in five years, and the weakness reflects thin coverage and an absence of news rather than deteriorating fundamentals.

Evidence: Solid State's momentum, axis by axis. Guidance, estimates, narrative and technicals are all flat or negative; only valuation scores well (table below).

Evidence: peers. The peers with momentum have it from three narratives: the industrial restock, data-centre demand and defence frameworks. In the market's mind Solid State belongs to none of the three; in fact it belongs to all three.

Inference. Momentum is nil or negative on every axis by construction, not because the business has deteriorated: the broker base is too thin to generate revisions, the company does not pre-empt orders, and the price has moved without news. That pattern is the signature of a bottoming stock. It is also why the dashboard's letters (D, D, A) describe the past correctly and forecast poorly: they measure what has happened to a price whose moves are 99% idiosyncratic.

So what. Richard is not paying for momentum; he is paying for its absence, in a stock whose peers have momentum on narratives that Solid State shares in substance. The December read-across cuts both ways: discoverIE (2 December) and Cohort (10 December) report before Solid State (15 December), and the market will apply a strong restock or defence-order message from them to Solid State's Components and Systems divisions immediately, just as it would apply a weak one.

Strongest counter-case. Negative momentum in an illiquid AIM share, in a market that is selling small, levered or illiquid names first, can persist for quarters with no fundamental cause and no fundamental cure. The stock's own history (moves of 10% to 20% on no news) says that a further fall before the interim would be normal, not exceptional.

What would change my view. Up: the price regaining the 200-day moving average (about 174p) on volume after the November update; a first positive revision from a second broker. Down: a close below the 52-week low (135p) before the interim, which would say that the market is pricing the deferral at more than an even chance.

Against the market. The market's momentum scores are correct, and I would not argue with them; the disagreement is about what they mean. For a stock whose multiple moves on its own events, the absence of momentum is the entry condition, not the warning.

Score: 25. No guidance or estimate momentum, a negative narrative and technical picture (price below all moving averages, relative strength in the bottom third), and peers enjoying momentum in narratives the stock shares in fact but not in the market's mind.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Key messageThe case is simple, because one driver decides it, and risky, because that driver is sudden, cannot be tracked through the company's own disclosures, and is worth a third to a half of a year's EPS. Track the Ministry, not the company.

Simplicity. The case has one driver that matters (Systems programme revenue against a fixed overhead), two dated gates (the interim margin and the April pre-close), and a nearly deterministic path below the operating line (interest of about £0.9m and falling, tax at 25%, 57.8m shares, no buyback, no acquisitions). Every link from the company's words to EPS can be traced except two: the quantity and date of Systems programme revenue, which the Ministry sets, and the channel margin, which the partner sets. That is as simple as a forecast gets, and the simplicity is also the fragility.

Fragilities, assumptions and requirements. The base case needs seven things to hold (table below); the first is the one that decides the case.

Suddenness, predictability, trackability, prevalence and materiality of share-price risks. The dominant risk, a tranche deferral, scores badly on every dimension except one: it is simple to understand (figure below). The risks also cluster: a deferral triggers under-absorbed overhead, inventory obsolescence and questions about working capital and accounting at the same time, so the correlated downside exceeds any single item.

Sentiment risks are common and partly realised already: UK procurement headlines, outflows from AIM small caps, peer read-across in December, memory-price headlines, the optical fall in H1 revenue, and a Capital Markets Day limited to frameworks. Liquidity and covenants sit outside the range of risks: the balance sheet can carry an FY25-type year with room to spare, and free cash flow rises in a deferral year as working capital unwinds, as FY25's 173% cash conversion showed.

Sector and cyclical precedents: awards, not budgets. Shares of qualified defence component suppliers follow the timing of awards, not budgets. Solid State's revenue fell 23% and its EPS expectations 60% in 2024 to 2025; Cohort's results depend on a ministry that provides 40% to 48% of its revenue; Chemring's Roke unit sat at 54% order cover; General Dynamics expected a Bowman contract "within six months" of September 2025, and the Morpheus programme has been extended repeatedly.

Sector and cyclical precedents: fixed-cost manufacturers. Fixed-cost manufacturers see margins fall hardest in downturns and recover hardest at the turn: Renishaw's margin fell from 24.1% to 15.7%; XP Power's rose from 4.3% to 7.9% in a year; Solid State's fell from 10.4% to 4.8%. The sector note's rule is to own asset-light designers through the cycle and to buy fixed-cost manufacturers at the turn.

Sector and cyclical precedents: restock, false friends and dispersion. The restock pulse runs six to eighteen months, and only designed-in parts reprice. The "false friend" pattern (TT Electronics' inventory-driven cash conversion of 150%; XP Power's capitalised development) is the sector's recurring cause of underperformance. Across the cohort, 18-month EPS outcomes around forecasts that rested on one or two awards ranged from about −40% to +25%, with awards late more often than early; Solid State's FY25 and FY26 are one of the wider pairs in that set.

The range of outcomes and its skew. FY27 EPS ranges from 7p to 12p around 10.8p, skewed down; FY28 EPS ranges from 11p to 17.5p around 14.0p, skewed up (chart below). The share price ranges from −45% to +50% over 18 months: skewed up in expectation and bimodal in shape. Predictability is low period by period and moderate in total, because what one period loses the next recovers; a two-year outcome outside 11p to 17p of FY28 EPS is less likely than the single-period volatility suggests.

So what. Size the position for the drawdown, not for the expectation. Treat the December margin and the April pre-close as the two points at which the range of outcomes narrows sharply. Monitor the Ministry's contract notices, RM6393 call-offs and Persistent Systems' releases rather than waiting for the company, because the company reports deliveries while the awards are announced elsewhere.

Strongest counter-case to the riskiness view. The fragility is overstated, for five reasons. The deferral has already been priced once and partly twice: the multiple is at the first percentile, and the price implies a 40% to 45% deferral probability. The order book covers two-thirds of FY27 revenue before the tranche. Power's revenue is the best-covered line in the group. The balance sheet turns a bad year into a cash-generative one. And in this company's history a deferred order has been a deferred order, reinstated four months later with a 20% EPS upgrade.

What would change my view. Toward lower risk: a disclosed programme or support share of Systems revenue; a renewal of the Persistent Systems agreement on stated terms; a second large customer; forward cover on the dollar. Toward higher risk: a Treasury decision deferring the plan's conventional lines; an adjustment to inventory or work in progress; net debt above £8m excluding leases at the interim.

Against the market. The market has priced the suddenness and under-priced the simplicity. It treats the stock as a lumpy defence supplier with a bad memory, and has not been shown that the lump is one revenue line with a known gearing, two dated gates and a balance sheet that absorbs a miss. I agree the case is risky. I think it is more trackable than the price implies, provided the investor tracks the Ministry and not the company.

Score: 35. A simple, traceable, one-driver case whose single driver is sudden, untrackable in advance and worth a third to a half of a year's EPS, in a sector whose precedents say awards slip more often than not; mitigated by a clean balance sheet, a covered first half and a multiple that has already priced much of the fear.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Key messageBottoming, at the boundary with Turning up: the multiple has bottomed on fear of an estimate cut that has not happened, so the next three events decide whether the bottom completes by confirmation or by a cut.

Evidence: where the stock sits now. By the dashboard's rule the starting phase is Bottoming. The two-year-forward P/E is 11.45x, against a ten-year tenth percentile of 10.9x and a ten-year median of 14.1x; on the five-year series today's multiple is at the first percentile (median 15.7x). The price is below every moving average, with relative strength in the bottom third. The 52-week low of 135p was set when forward estimates were lower than today's, and the December 2024 low was 123p.

Evidence: the fundamentals have turned. Estimates sit at their post-upgrade level of June 2026 and have not been rebased. The dividend was raised 10%, the underlying order book is £18m higher, three divisions grew in FY26, the destock has ended, and the company has not warned.

Evidence: the last cycle. The multiple was 15x to 19x through the FY22 to FY24 delivery years. The November 2024 deferral caused a 40% collapse in the price, during which the multiple expanded on cut earnings. The shares rebuilt to 199p by June 2026 on the order's reinstatement and on delivery, and have fallen 18% since on timing fear, with estimates flat.

Inference. The stock is bottoming in an unusual way: the multiple has bottomed on fear of an estimate cut that has not happened. A textbook bottom combines rebased estimates with a cheap multiple; this one combines unrebased estimates with an even cheaper multiple. The next move therefore depends on whether the estimates are cut, which would complete the bottom the hard way with a second fall toward 85p to 120p, or confirmed, which would skip the rebasing and move the stock straight to Turning up on unchanged numbers.

The fundamentals (the order book, the divisions, the end of the destock and the capacity built) are already in the Turning-up phase, and the price is not; the gap between them is both the opportunity and the timing risk. The price implies a deferral probability of roughly 40% to 45%, against Viewforth's 20% (summary point 6): a market that sees two possible outcomes, and has watched this company suffer a deferral once, prices the deferral almost as a coin toss.

Where the phase moves next. A confirmed tranche (in the November update, in a regulatory announcement, or through Systems revenue above £30m in a half) moves the stock from Bottoming to Turning up on unchanged numbers. A shipped tranche, a utilisation figure and a first NATO follow-on together move it to Broadening and reinforcing, the sovereign-platform archetype in which the multiple recovers toward its delivery-phase range of 14x to 16x. A failed margin test or a stated second-half slip returns it to the November 2024 template, a Collapsing phase from which the last recovery took four months to begin and eighteen months to complete.

So what. The phase argues for the guideline multiple (12.7x, between the crash and conservative bands) today, and for the ten-year median (14.1x) once the first tranche is confirmed. It argues against paying for the delivery-phase range until Ashchurch is visibly loading. It also argues that the asymmetric moment is now, before the first of the three events, because a bottoming stock with unrebased estimates re-rates faster on confirmation than one whose estimates have already been rebased.

Strongest counter-case. Bottoming phases with unrebased estimates more often resolve by rebasing than by confirmation. The price fell 18% on no news because holders below the 3% disclosure threshold have concluded that the tranche is late. Sector precedents say awards slip more often than not. And the stock's technical picture (below a falling 50-day average, relative strength at the 33rd percentile) is that of a stock still searching for its low, not one that has found it.

What would change my view. Toward Turning up: an order book above £100m in November, with a tranche or second-half weighting named; an interim margin above 5.5%. Toward Collapsing: a stated deferral, an interim margin below 5%, or a close below 135p.

Against the market. The market's implied probability of a deferral is about double Viewforth's. I agree with the dashboard's phase (Bottoming), and I place the stock at the upper boundary of that phase, because the fundamentals have already turned and only the price and the estimates have not.

Score: 55. Bottoming at the boundary with turning up: the multiple at its own first percentile has priced roughly double our probability of a deferral, the fundamentals have turned, and the estimates have not yet been tested, so the next three events decide whether the bottom completes by confirmation or by rebasing.

11The fair multiple

Key messageThe 12.7x guideline is fair today and will be too low once the first tranche is confirmed: 14.1x on confirmation, and 15x to 16x only when Ashchurch utilisation and a NATO follow-on are both visible.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a stock in the Bottoming phase is the 30th percentile of its own ten-year two-year-forward P/E range: 12.70x, 11% above the 11.45x the stock trades on now. The ten-year bands around the guideline are 10.9x (tenth percentile, "crash"), 13.1x (35th, "conservative"), 14.1x (median, "prudent"), 16.2x (75th, "defendable") and 18.4x (90th, "mania"). The five-year range is 10.5x to 23.3x, with a median of 15.7x and an interquartile range of 14.0x to 17.1x.

My view: four reasons the guideline is right today.

  • The multiple is driven by the company. With an R-squared of 1%, the stock's own history is the right frame, not the cohort's 17x to 22x. The quality names' ratings are a ceiling the stock has not sustained in five years, not a level it will be pulled toward.
  • The forecasts have not been tested. FY29 consensus is one broker's estimate, the base case sits above it, and the next two events can cut the numbers. A multiple between the crash and conservative bands is the right price for that uncertainty.
  • The earnings base is less clean than the adjusted figure suggests. Reported EPS is about 3.6p below adjusted EPS in FY27 (7.2p against 10.8p), a gap that narrows to 3.0p by FY31 as amortisation of acquired intangibles runs off, and about 0.6p a year of recurring reorganisation cost is excluded by convention. On reported earnings the stock trades on about 22x FY27, so the "cheap" label depends on the basis, as it does for every peer.
  • Liquidity is thin. The register is thin and only about £0.3m of shares trade a day, which earns a liquidity discount in the current market regardless of fundamentals.

My view: three reasons the guideline will be too low on confirmation.

  • The stock's own history. The stock held 14x to 16x through FY22 to FY24, when it was a smaller, less accredited and more acquisitive business, with no Ashchurch site and no three-division structure. The delivery-phase range exists in the stock's own history.
  • The enterprise-value cross-check. At about £96m of enterprise value, the stock trades on about 7.0x FY27 and 5.8x FY28 base-case EBITDA, against 11x to 12x EBITA paid for Trival and 3Gmetalworx and 25.9x operating profit for Gooch & Housego. 10x FY28 EBITDA would be about £166m of enterprise value, roughly 280p a share: the category's deal prices set a floor on value, even if not on the daily price.
  • The unpriced cash option. Net cash arrives by March 2028 and reaches about £16m by FY31, with no stated plan for using it. A buyback would be worth 8% to 12% of EPS, and would also lift the multiple the market pays for a company that has shown it can allocate capital.

Where I would put the multiple, phase by phase. 12.7x while the stock is Bottoming (now); 14.1x, the ten-year median, when a tranche is confirmed and the phase turns up; 15x to 16x only when Ashchurch utilisation and a NATO follow-on are both visible, the reinforcing phase. In the deferral case the multiple applied to depressed current-year earnings expands, as it did in November 2024 (17x a cut number), but the price falls. The fair trough multiple is 10.9x to 12x on whatever the forward earnings become, which is why the deferral range is 85p to 120p and not lower.

Strongest counter-case. A stock that has never earned a sustained premium, with a margin at the bottom of its cohort, one broker's forecasts beyond FY28, a bill-and-hold judgement among its key audit matters, and a channel partner that could remove its best business, should trade at a structural discount to its own history. The market's refusal to pay more than 11x after a published plan, a CAIN award and a 10% dividend rise is evidence that the discount has become structural rather than cyclical.

What would change my view. Up: a confirmed tranche (to 14.1x); a capital-allocation framework or buyback; a second broker publishing FY29 EPS above 16p. Down: a stated deferral (to 10.9x on a cut number); an accounting event, which would damage the multiple more than the cash.

Against the market. The house broker quotes about 15x forward earnings against 18.2x for UK defence and industrial technology, and calls the discount unjustified. I think the discount to peers is partly justified (by scale, liquidity, one-broker coverage, and a sub-tier position with a supplier dependency), while the discount to the stock's own history is not. That is a narrower and more defensible claim, and it is the claim the guideline multiple makes.

Score: 68. The guideline 12.7x is fair for the Bottoming phase and 11% above the current multiple, with the stock's own median (14.1x) available on confirmation of one contract and a takeover floor at roughly 10x EBITDA well above the current price; the multiple is low for company-specific reasons that company-specific events can reverse.

12Total shareholder return, via the Dupont framework

Key messageThe 18-month return is a re-rating paid in steps on dated events; the three-year return is an earnings return that survives a one-year deferral.

The model's return at the guideline multiple. Measured from the model's starting price of 171p (see end-notes), the 18-month return to 30 September 2027 is +44.3% (+47.9% annualised), for a value of 247p a share: dividends contribute +1.8%, the change in multiple +36.9% and earnings +4.1%. The three-year return to 31 March 2029 is +72.3% (+25.0% annualised), for a value of 295p a share: dividends contribute +6.0%, the multiple +12.5% and earnings +47.8%. Measured from today's 162.5p, the two values are +52% and +82% before dividends.

What drives the 18-month return: the multiple. Moving from the first percentile of the stock's own range to its 30th percentile is worth about 37 points. Earnings add about 4 points, because the base case has FY27 EPS below FY26 and the forward earnings the market will capitalise in September 2027 are the FY28 and FY29 figures of 14.0p and 17.7p. The 3.0p dividend adds under 2 points.

The 18-month return is therefore a re-rating return. In a stock whose multiple moves on its own events, a re-rating return arrives in steps on specific dates: the November order book, the December margin, a contract announcement and the April pre-close. The return does not accrue gradually; it is paid on confirmation.

Weighting the three paths at 55%, 25% and 20% (base case 247p; award-led 230p to 300p, taken as 265p; deferral 85p to 120p, taken as 95p) gives a probability-weighted 18-month value of about 220p, roughly +35% from 162.5p. The distribution is bimodal: better than +50% in four cases out of five, and about −40% in the fifth.

What drives the three-year return: earnings. Adjusted EPS rises from 11.0p in FY26, through 14.0p and 17.7p, to about 20p of forward earnings by March 2029, a near-doubling to which the model attributes 48 points. The multiple adds 12.5 points (the same move to 12.7x, spread over a longer period), and dividends of 3.0p, 3.4p and 3.9p (about 10.3p in total) add 6 points.

The three-year return is what Richard is paid for being right about the business rather than about the date, and it is far more robust to a deferral than the 18-month return. In the deferral path, FY28 and FY29 earnings arrive a year late rather than not at all, because in this company's record a deferred order has been reinstated, not lost. The three-year value in that path is therefore perhaps 220p to 240p rather than 95p, and the probability-weighted three-year value sits close to the base case's 295p.

The sensitivities in Judgements 1 and 2 apply directly to the three-year value: each £10m of Systems programme revenue in FY28 is worth about 3.9p of EPS and, at 12.7x, about 50p a share; each two points of overhead growth is worth about 1.4p of EPS and about 18p a share.

What is not in the return. Five sources of value are excluded, and all but the currency effect are upside:

  • No buyback: a £10m repurchase at the current price would add about 10% to EPS from FY29.
  • No acquisition.
  • No re-rating beyond the 30th percentile: the ten-year median multiple would add about 28p to the 18-month value.
  • No takeover: the category's 10x to 12x EBITA would imply roughly 280p on FY28 base-case EBITDA.
  • No currency effect: about ±0.4p of EPS across the range of brokers' sterling forecasts.

Strongest counter-case. A return that is 37 points of multiple in 18 months depends on the one thing the company cannot time. It must be earned in a market that refuses re-ratings, in an AIM stock trading £0.3m a day, from investors who have already declined to re-rate the shares on a published plan and a delivered first order. If the tranche slips past April 2027, the 18-month return is negative even though the three-year return survives.

What would change my view. The same gates as in sections 10 and 11: the November order book, the December margin and Systems revenue, a contract announcement, and the April pre-close. Only a second deferral or a structural event (in the channel, or an accounting adjustment) would change the three-year return.

Against the market. The sell side's targets (a 288p mean; Cavendish 301p; an earlier Zeus fair value of 330p) are above the model's 18-month value, and the brokers reach them by applying a peer multiple to their own forecasts. The model reaches 247p by applying the stock's own 30th-percentile multiple to forecasts that are below consensus this year and above it next, which is a more conservative route to a similar place. I agree with the market on the destination and disagree on the mechanism and the date.

Score: 70. A +44% 18-month return at the guideline multiple (about +52% from today's price) that is almost entirely a dated, event-driven re-rating from the first percentile, and a +72% three-year return that is almost entirely earnings and is robust to a one-year deferral; favourable in expectation (about +35% probability-weighted over 18 months), bimodal in shape.

13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

The business. Solid State is a sound, narrow, under-earning business in the right end-markets at the right time. Honest operators run it; they built the capacity before the orders came and are now waiting, like the shareholders, for a ministry to sign.

The business case is better than the market has been told. Three divisions are growing on three independent clocks, the recurring base is £131m and rising, the gross margin is reliable and improving, the balance sheet turns to net cash within eighteen months, and each £10m of defence programme revenue that lands in the built facility is worth a third of this year's earnings.

The investment case is more fragile than the business case. The one revenue line that sets the variance is the one line the company cannot time; the multiple will move on nothing else; and the sell side has not rebased its estimates. The next three events will therefore either confirm the estimates while the multiple is at a trough, or cut them while it is at a trough.

The expectation is favourable and the shape is bimodal. Measured from 162.5p, the return is about +35% probability-weighted over 18 months; +52% in the base case, at a multiple that is still only the stock's own 30th percentile; and +82% over three years, mostly from earnings and robust to a one-year slip. Against that sits a one-in-five chance of a 40% fall. The price implies roughly a 40% to 45% probability of deferral, against Viewforth's 20%; that gap is the investment case, and the three events of the next eight weeks test it.

The constructive posture. Size the position for the drawdown. Hold the three-year earnings case as the anchor. Treat the November order book, the December margin and the April pre-close as the gates through which the 18-month re-rating must pass.

C

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: C. Structural, well-aimed defence demand and a cyclical industrial turn meet internal changes that are coherent and pre-funded but carry no financial force of their own, and the conversion of both runs on a government calendar the company does not set.

C

Foundations' Robustness: C. A genuine accreditation and design-in moat, a reliable gross margin and a clean balance sheet are set against a sole-source channel partner with undisclosed terms, a 17% customer, a 39% distribution leg with no moat, unhedged dollar purchasing and a margin and return profile at the bottom of the cohort.

C

Setups' Fit/Crispness: C. Closest to "CfC in quality cyclical at trough-on-trough, leading to reversion to normal" (a first-percentile multiple on a 6% margin against a 9% normal, with a dated and resolvable cause for concern), but the quality is medium, the cycle is a ministry's calendar rather than the economy's, and the estimates are unrebased, so the fit is real and not crisp.

D

Case Riskiness: D. One simple, traceable driver whose timing is sudden, untrackable in advance and worth a third to a half of a year's EPS, in a sector whose precedent is that awards slip more often than not, partly offset by a balance sheet that absorbs a bad year and a multiple that has already priced much of the fear.

Bases and definitions

Solid State's financial year runs to 31 March; FY27 is the year to 31 March 2027. Profit figures are on the company's adjusted basis, which is also the brokers' basis and the basis of FactSet consensus: adjusted operating profit is stated before amortisation of acquired intangibles, share-based payments and reorganisation costs. "Consensus" is the FactSet median at 22 October 2026; it rests on one visible broker (Cavendish) for FY27 and FY28 and on one broker for FY29. The company's own "market expectations" figure is the average of Cavendish, Berenberg and Zeus. "The base case" is the Financial Analyst's model (update 1), whose forecasts this memo uses throughout. AIM is the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market; the LTIP is the company's long-term incentive plan.

Starting price and return horizons

The model's return calculation was struck at 171p, the previous close. Returns measured from today's 162.5p are correspondingly higher: for example, +52% rather than +44% over 18 months, and +82% rather than +72% over three years (before dividends). The split of total shareholder return into dividends, multiple and earnings is the model template's own; its arithmetic should not be reconciled with the forward multiples quoted elsewhere in this memo. The two horizons end on the model's fixed column dates (30 September 2027 and 31 March 2029), not 18 months and three years from today.

Note on the forecast inputs

I change no forecast input. The evidence assembled since the second set of analysis offsets itself within the 55% weighting the base case already places on the H2 FY27 tranche. On the positive side sit the published plan naming CAIN, the £727m framework vehicle and the Segmented Acquisition Model's one-year lane; on the negative side sit the £28bn funding gap, the possible delay to the spending review, the CMA screening, the United States continuing resolution and the Capital Markets Day's "no new financial information". Nothing in that evidence bears on the overhead, gross-margin, cash-flow or below-the-line inputs. The input I would most readily move is the FY27 second-half revenue growth of 13.1%, if the November trading update carries a warning that FY27 is weighted to the second half or the interim margin prints below 5.5%; until then, the probability-weighted inputs are the right ones to hold.
